questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why 0 is not prime
questions.learningObjective: explain why 0 is not prime
questions.stem: In a city planner's memo, the count of vacant lots is 0 for one district, and the memo asks why 0 is not a prime number. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Every nonzero whole number divides 0 evenly, since 0 divided by any nonzero number gives 0, so 0 has infinitely many positive factors. A prime number must have exactly two distinct positive factors, and 0 has far more, so it cannot be prime. It is not composite either, because composite numbers are defined among the whole numbers greater than 1. The trap is to argue that 0 times any number equals 0, which is a property of zero and has nothing to do with how many factors a number has.

questions.explanation: Every nonzero whole number divides 0, so 0 has infinitely many positive factors and cannot have exactly two as a prime must. The trap is the fact that 0 times anything is 0.
questions.hint: Ask how many positive numbers divide 0 exactly.

questions.topic: Irrational number written as a square root

questions.stem: A city planner's memo explains why a diagonal of a unit square in the new plaza is given as the square root of 2 rather than a decimal. Explain why that diagonal is not a fraction.

answer.exemplar: The diagonal of a unit square has length the square root of 2, because the sum of the squares of the legs equals the square of the diagonal, and 1 plus 1 equals 2. If that length were a fraction, say a over b, then a over b squared would equal 2, so a squared would equal 2 b squared, which is impossible because the left side has an odd number of factors of 2 and the right side has an even number. The trap is to think that because the diagonal can be measured to many decimal places, it must be a fraction, but a decimal approximation is not the exact value.

questions.explanation: No fraction of whole numbers squares to 2, so the diagonal of a unit square cannot be written as a fraction. The trap is to trust a long decimal approximation.
questions.hint: Ask whether any fraction of whole numbers squares to 2.

questions.topic: Why 1 is neither prime nor composite
questions.learningObjective: explain why the two definitions exclude 1
questions.stem: A city planner's memo records a block numbered 1 and notes that this number is neither prime nor composite. Explain why the classification excludes it.

answer.exemplar: A prime number has exactly two distinct positive factors, 1 and itself, and a composite number has more than two positive factors. The number 1 has only one positive factor, the number 1 itself, so it fails the prime test because it does not have two factors, and it fails the composite test because it does not have more than two. The two definitions together cover only the whole numbers greater than 1, and 1 sits outside both of them. The trap is to argue that 1 is prime because multiplying by 1 leaves other numbers unchanged, but that is a statement about the multiplicative identity rather than about factors.

questions.explanation: One has exactly one positive factor, so it fails the prime rule of exactly two and the composite rule of more than two. The trap is to treat its role in multiplication as primality.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Odd exponent on a negative base
questions.learningObjective: explain why an odd power keeps a negative sign
questions.stem: A city planner's memo explains that a survey line runs negative 4 metres below datum and that the plan cubes the depth. Explain why the memo records a negative result.

answer.exemplar: Cubing negative 4 multiplies three negative factors, so the signs combine to a single negative sign and the value is negative 64. An odd power always leaves one negative sign unpaired, so the result of the memo's rule must be negative whenever the base is negative. The trap is to reason from squaring, where two negative signs cancel and the result is positive, and to expect the same cancellation here. Squaring and cubing differ in exactly this one respect, and the memo depends on the difference to keep track of which side of datum a line sits on.

questions.explanation: Cubing negative 4 uses three negative signs, so one sign survives and the result is negative 64. The trap is to carry over the cancellation seen in squaring.
questions.hint: Count the negative signs used by a power of 3.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Opposite of a number
questions.learningObjective: explain how the opposite of a change is found
questions.stem: A memo from the city planner records a zoning change of negative 130 metres on one boundary and asks what the opposite change would be. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The opposite of a number is found by moving the same distance from zero in the other direction, so the opposite of negative 130 metres is positive 130 metres. The sign records which way the boundary shifted, and the opposite shift would move it the same number of metres in the other direction, leaving the size unchanged. This is why opposite pairs such as negative 130 and positive 130 always add to zero. The trap is to read the opposite as doubling the change, or as reversing the sign without keeping the size, and to think that an opposite of a negative number might be a smaller number.

questions.explanation: The opposite of negative 130 is positive 130, because an opposite keeps the size and flips the direction, and the two sum to zero. The trap is to change the magnitude too.
questions.hint: Reflect the change across zero on the number line.

questions.learningObjective: justify why a number is composite

answer.exemplar: A composite number is a whole number greater than 1 that has more than two positive factors, and 60 fits that description because it can be written as 6 times 10, or as 4 times 15, and in fact has twelve positive factors. Any whole number greater than 1 that is not prime is composite, and 60 splits into two smaller whole numbers, which is exactly what makes it composite. The trap is to think that a number has to be written in some special way to count as composite, when any splitting into two whole numbers greater than 1 is enough. The numbers 1 and 0 are excluded from the composite class for separate reasons.

questions.explanation: 60 splits into whole numbers greater than 1, such as 6 times 10, and it has twelve positive factors, so it is composite. The trap is thinking composite numbers need a special form.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Definition of a prime number
questions.learningObjective: justify in writing that a number is prime
questions.stem: A memo from the city planner explains that a plot number of 53 is prime and asks a reader to justify the claim in writing. Explain why 53 is prime.

answer.exemplar: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive factors are 1 and the number itself, and 53 fits that description exactly. To check it, divide 53 by every prime up to its square root, which is a little over 7, so the only candidates are 2, 3, 5 and 7. It divides by none of them evenly, since 53 is odd, the digit sum of 8 is not a multiple of 3, it does not end in 0 or 5, and 7 times 7 is 49 with a remainder of 4. With no further factor possible, 53 is prime. The trap is stopping after the first oddness test, since many odd numbers such as 21 and 35 are still composite.

questions.explanation: 53 divides by none of 2, 3, 5 or 7, the only primes below its square root, so its only positive factors are 1 and 53 and it is prime. The trap is that oddness alone leaves out 21 and 35.
questions.hint: Test 53 against the primes up to its square root.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rational number written as a terminating decimal
questions.learningObjective: explain why a terminating decimal is exact
questions.stem: A city planning memo explains that a share of 1 over 5 of a hectare can be published as the decimal 0.2. Explain why that decimal is exact rather than an approximation.

answer.exemplar: One fifth equals 0.2 exactly, because the denominator 5 is a prime factor of 10, so 0.2 can be scaled back to 1 over 5 without any leftover. A terminating decimal is always a rational number written in a place-value form, and writing a rational number in that form loses nothing. The memo can therefore print 0.2 on the public notice and every reader can recover the exact fraction. The trap is to treat a short decimal as a rounded guess, when the length of the decimal has no bearing on whether the value is exact; a fraction such as 1 over 3 repeats for ever and is just as exact as 0.2 but is not finite.

questions.explanation: One fifth equals 0.2 exactly, because the denominator 5 divides a power of 10, so the decimal is a rational number in place-value form. The trap is treating a short decimal as a rounded guess.
questions.hint: Multiply 0.2 by 5 and see what you get.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why 1 is neither prime nor composite
questions.learningObjective: explain why a trivial factorisation proves nothing
questions.stem: A city planner's memo shows 91 written as 1 times 91 and asks why this factorisation does not make 91 composite, since 1 is not prime. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A composite number is one that can be written as a product of two whole numbers greater than 1, and 91 equals 7 times 13, so 91 is composite. The factorisation 1 times 91 does not count, because the factor 1 is not greater than 1, and 1 is neither prime nor composite, so it cannot serve as one of the two factors. This is exactly why 1 is excluded from both classes, and why the number 1 itself is never called composite even though it can be written as 1 times 1. The trap is to think that any product of two whole numbers proves compositeness, when the rule requires both factors to be greater than 1.

questions.explanation: The factorisation 1 times 91 does not count, because a composite number needs two factors greater than 1, and 1 is not one. Any product of two whole numbers looks like a split, but the rule excludes 1.
questions.hint: Check whether each factor in the split is greater than 1.
